what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Agents, fragile infrastructure and spreadsheet risk are colliding
sections.para: A first draft of a conference talk argues three problems arrive at once: agents as the insider threat that never scaled, infrastructure designed for none of it, and risk management on spreadsheets at quarterly speed. Together they leave companies blind and slow. The way out carries an irony: constraining an agent lets you trust it with more autonomy.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Three known problems combine into one insider scenario
sections.para: Agents are reasoning engines with tools and skills, harmful even without malice. Infrastructure lacks journals, unified identity and least privilege, and fails on its own, as the largest cloud outages showed. Risk management on spreadsheets cannot see reach, so it cannot fund controls and the plug gets pulled. Brakes are what let a car go fast.

sections.label: One: the ultimate insider
sections.line: An agent is an insider with every skill
sections.para: Human and code insiders were bounded by hours, conscience or static logic; an agent is a model in a loop with tools and every skill. Incidents include Replit deleting a production database, Gemini CLI destroying files, Amazon Q's injected wipe prompt, EchoLeak, and an espionage campaign where Claude did 80 to 90 per cent of the work.

sections.label: Two: the infrastructure that cannot hold them
sections.line: Business infrastructure cannot recover, identify or contain agents
sections.para: Four gaps: no journaling and daily backups, unmanaged non-human identity, permissions that are the union of everything (workloads use under 5 per cent of grants), and fragile containment, shown by the fourteen-hour AWS DNS outage and Cloudflare's configuration failure. Zero-days like ToolShell dissolve controls, and internal systems lack adversarial antibodies.

sections.label: Three: risk management at the speed of spreadsheets
sections.line: Spreadsheet risk management decides too slowly to fund controls
sections.para: 48 per cent of organisations track risk in spreadsheets, reviewed quarterly, when agent decisions need seconds and pre-approved envelopes. Without seeing reach, nobody can judge appetite or fund controls. Gartner predicts over 40 per cent of agentic projects cancelled by 2027; the plug comes out when nobody can stop or recover.

sections.label: Why we do not see more of it
sections.line: Agent incidents go unseen because nobody has to report
sections.para: Aviation's confidential reporting system takes about 100,000 reports a year, 1.8 million so far, protected from use against the reporter. Cyber has nothing similar: CIRCIA's final rule slipped to September 2026. Verizon's 2025 report shows the human element in about 60 per cent of breaches, and the unreported column is likely worse.

sections.label: The collision
sections.line: Together they form one nightmare already in the record
sections.para: An entity acting as employee, user and API at machine speed, infrastructure that cannot stop it or replay to before, and a decision process that sees nothing until a spreadsheet row afterwards. Every piece is in eighteen months of public record, just reported separately as different kinds of news.

sections.label: The other half: the way out, and the irony
sections.line: Constraining agents is what lets you grant them autonomy
sections.para: The way out: write down reach, mandate, gap and barriers in an Agent Behaviour Policy, where only a boundary is a control. Contain in layers with identity per agent and journaling twins, watch in real time, decide in advance through a licence to operate and expiring risk acceptance, and prove provenance. Brakes make speed survivable.

sections.label: How this might become a talk
sections.line: A forty-minute talk in three acts and a turn
sections.para: The proposed talk runs three acts: the insider, the infrastructure and the spreadsheet, then turns to disclosure and the way out. It would take forty minutes, one figure per act with sourced evidence, aimed at security conferences, risk and audit audiences, and boards. Organisers are asked which act they want more of.

sections.label: Sources
sections.line: Sources: the reports, incidents and studies cited
sections.para: Sources include Ponemon's 2025 Cost of Insider Risks, Anthropic's agent and espionage reports, Simon Willison's lethal trifecta, the Replit, Gemini CLI, Amazon Q and EchoLeak incidents, CyberArk, Microsoft, AWS and Cloudflare outage analyses, Gartner, MIT NANDA, NASA ASRS, CIRCIA and Verizon's 2025 DBIR.
